title: Withdrawal on cessation but controlled use = physical dependence (not opioid use disorder)
vignette: An 18-year-old woman comes to the office to discuss her pain medication. Five months ago, the patient fractured her vertebrae in a ski accident, requiring surgery and prolonged postsurgical rehabilitation. Since the accident, she has been prescribed hydrocodone/acetaminophen 4 times a day for pain. The patient's pain is adequately controlled and does not interfere with day-to-day activities. Over the past month, she has tried to stop the medication, but each time she develops rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and vomiting, requiring her to take it to relieve the discomfort. The patient has reduced hydrocodone/acetaminophen intake from 4 to 3 times daily and cannot reduce it further due to these symptoms. She is anxious and frustrated about not being able to discontinue it. Urine drug screen is positive for hydrocodone only. A review of the state prescription drug monitoring database reveals no other controlled substances or irregularities. Which of the following best describes this patient's condition?

clues.text: prescribed hydrocodone/acetaminophen 4 times a day for pain
clues.note: She is on chronic, appropriately prescribed opioid therapy for a legitimate indication - the setting in which physical dependence commonly develops.

clues.text: pain is adequately controlled and does not interfere with day-to-day activities
clues.note: Controlled use without functional impairment or compulsive drug-seeking argues AGAINST opioid use disorder.

clues.text: tried to stop the medication, but each time she develops rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and vomiting
clues.note: Rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and vomiting on discontinuation are classic OPIOID WITHDRAWAL symptoms - the defining feature of PHYSICAL DEPENDENCE.
No other/aberrant substances and a clean prescription-monitoring review indicate controlled, as-prescribed use (not misuse or use disorder).

whatMatters: She develops WITHDRAWAL (rhinorrhea, lacrimation, vomiting) when stopping a chronically prescribed opioid, but her use is CONTROLLED with no impairment, misuse, or aberrant behavior. Withdrawal on cessation with otherwise controlled use = PHYSICAL DEPENDENCE. Answer C.
strategy: Distinguish four concepts. PHYSICAL DEPENDENCE = withdrawal symptoms on cessation/dose reduction (physiologic adaptation), use remains controlled - fits here. TOLERANCE = needing more drug for the same effect (her dose isn't escalating). OPIOID USE DISORDER = compulsive, uncontrolled use despite harm (absent - no impairment, clean monitoring). MISUSE = using differently than prescribed/diverting (absent - urine positive for hydrocodone only).

eliminations.label: Misuse - no aberrant use
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: using an opioid other than as prescribed (overuse, using for non-pain reasons, obtaining from multiple sources). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she takes it exactly as prescribed, urine is positive for hydrocodone only, and monitoring is clean. ✅ Correct if: taking extra doses, doctor-shopping, or using for anxiety/euphoria.

eliminations.label: Opioid use disorder - use is controlled
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a pattern of compulsive, UNCONTROLLED opioid use despite harmful social/occupational consequences. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: her use is controlled, pain-focused, without impairment or craving-driven behavior; she is actually trying to STOP. ✅ Correct if: loss of control, craving, continued use despite harm, neglecting responsibilities.

eliminations.label: Tolerance - dose isn't escalating
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: needing an INCREASED dose to achieve the same effect. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: her pain is controlled and she is reducing (not increasing) the dose; the problem is withdrawal on stopping, not diminishing effect. ✅ Correct if: progressive dose increases for the same analgesia.

reasoning: She is on chronic, appropriately prescribed opioid therapy with controlled use
Attempts to stop trigger withdrawal (rhinorrhea, lacrimation, vomiting)
There is no loss of control, misuse, aberrant behavior, or dose escalation
-> withdrawal on cessation with controlled use = physical dependence; answer C
mechanism: Chronic opioid therapy produces neuroadaptation. Opioids bind mu receptors and inhibit presynaptic release of pain neurotransmitters; with continued use, receptor DOWN-REGULATION and desensitization occur, so ABRUPT cessation or dose reduction unmasks a hyperactive state -> OPIOID WITHDRAWAL (rhinorrhea, lacrimation, yawning, sweating, piloerection, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, dysphoria). This is PHYSICAL DEPENDENCE: an expected physiologic adaptation defined by withdrawal on discontinuation, with use otherwise CONTROLLED. It is distinct from TOLERANCE (needing more drug for the same effect), OPIOID USE DISORDER (compulsive, uncontrolled use despite harm - a behavioral disorder), and MISUSE (using contrary to prescription). Management of physical dependence is a gradual, scheduled TAPER, often with pain-management support - not addiction treatment. This patient's controlled use, clean urine (hydrocodone only) and clean prescription-monitoring review confirm dependence rather than a use disorder.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Behavioral science > opioids: physical dependence = withdrawal on cessation (controlled use); tolerance = increased dose for same effect; opioid use disorder = uncontrolled use despite harm; misuse = using other than prescribed; manage dependence with taper.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Withdrawal on stopping + controlled use, no harm = physical dependence (not use disorder).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on physical dependence vs tolerance vs use disorder vs misuse, or opioid withdrawal signs? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Use disorder needs loss of control/harm (absent); tolerance needs dose escalation (absent); misuse needs aberrant use (urine hydrocodone-only).

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: withdrawal on cessation with controlled use = physical dependence; treat with scheduled taper.

memoryHook: Her body screams withdrawal when the opioid stops, but she never loses control or misuses it - that's physical dependence, not addiction; the fix is a slow taper.
